item.title: Tonga faces severe drought threat as El Niño brings very dry conditions nationwide

item.content:encoded:
Tonga is facing the prospect of a severe and prolonged drought, with the Tonga Meteorological Service warning that a strong to very strong El Niño could bring very dry conditions across the entire country and place growing pressure on water supplies, food production and public health.

The Meteorological Drought Outlook issued on 18 August 2026 says El Niño is already underway in Tonga and the tropical Pacific, with forecasts pointing to an event that could rank among the strongest observed since 1950. El Niño conditions typically bring below-average rainfall and the possibility of prolonged drought in Tonga.

The warning comes as Tonga is already experiencing widespread dryness. In July, dry conditions were observed across all of Tonga, with very dry conditions in Vava’u and seriously dry conditions in Tongatapu and ‘Eua. Over the three months from May to July, dry conditions were recorded across all island groups, with seriously dry conditions in Ha’apai, Tongatapu and ‘Eua.

The outlook for the coming months is even more concerning.

Very dry conditions are forecast across all of Tonga in August, with a 70 to 80 per cent chance in Niuafo’ou and Niuatoputapu, 50 to 70 per cent in Tongatapu and ‘Eua, and 40 to 50 per cent in Ha’apai and Vava’u.

For August to October, the chance of very dry conditions rises to between 80 and 100 per cent across all of Tonga.

The drought outlook shows the situation worsening in several island groups by the end of October. Niuafo’ou is forecast to move from Drought Alert to Drought Declaration, while Niuatoputapu is expected to remain under Drought Declaration after escalating from Drought Warning. Vava’u is forecast to progress from Drought Alert to Drought Declaration.

Ha’apai, Tongatapu and ‘Eua are already at Drought Declaration and are expected to remain there through October.

The outlook identifies reduced or empty water tanks within one month, followed by depleted groundwater, including on Tongatapu, and drying bore and well water. It also warns of increased costs for pumping and drinking water, as well as increased water salinity.

The impacts could become more severe if dry conditions persist, with competing demands for water from households, agriculture and livestock.

Agriculture is also expected to come under increasing pressure as soil moisture declines.

The Meteorological Service identifies impacts on yams, cassava and taro, along with reduced breadfruit and pineapple yields. Kava growth could be reduced, while cattle and pigs could also be affected by reduced pasture availability and increased demand for drinking water.

The outlook also warns of reduced crop production, higher crop prices, increased irrigation demand and impacts on livelihoods and food security.

The drought could also create serious health and hygiene problems.

The outlook identifies dehydration, skin disease, nose bleeding, fever, vomiting and breathing difficulties associated with prolonged drought. Reduced access to water for sanitation and hygiene could increase infectious diseases, including typhoid, diarrhoea and lung disease.

Vulnerable people, including people with disabilities in the outer islands, could face reduced access to water. The outlook also warns that hospitals and emergency centres could run out of water if the drought persists.

The effects could extend well beyond households and farms.

The Meteorological Service identifies potential disruption to household incomes and livelihoods, increased demands for drought relief, higher shipping costs and increased pressure on water facilities.

Schools could also be affected, particularly in the outer islands, with reduced water supplies potentially affecting students’ focus and performance. Prolonged drought could lead to lower attendance, dropouts and school closures.

The outlook also warns of an increased risk of wildfires, while power supplies could be disrupted by limited water available for cooling equipment. Fire Services may need to use seawater.

The Meteorological Service notes that the impacts are based on stakeholder consultation and are estimates of when impacts may become evident following below-average rainfall. The severity of impacts can vary according to island size, topography, geology and soil type.

With very dry conditions forecast across every island group and the drought outlook showing further escalation through October, the warning is that Tonga’s dry spell could become a much broader threat to water security, food production, health and livelihoods.

item.title: Prop idol has his 'mojo' back - and Wallabies want more
item.description: Wallabies coach Les Kiss will stay in regular touch with Taniela Tupou's French club to ensure the in-form prop remains a regular fixture. Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled how the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.
item.content:encoded:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss will stay in regular touch with Taniela Tupou's French club to ensure the in-form prop remains a regular fixture.

Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled how the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.

Tupou scored two first-half tries for Australia, who trailed before scoring 42 consecutive points in a 56-17 defeat of Japan in Townsville on Saturday.

All three starting front-rowers, as well as replacement hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa and back-rowers Harry Wilson and Charlie Cale, were Australia's try-scorers in Townsville.

Tupou scored the match-winner in Osaka against Eddie Jones' men a week earlier after coming off the bench and has shown power and skill to indicate he's back near his best approaching next year's home Rugby World Cup.

" He's found a little bit of himself again, and he's been more of himself," Wallabies coach Kiss said, while also noting his combination with good mate and returning lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto.

" I'm very, very big on making sure the players be themselves as much as possible."

Former Queensland Reds star Tupou agonised over his move from Australian rugby to France, with Racing 92 last season but it's helped him turn back the clock after several underwhelming seasons at the Melbourne Rebels and NSW Waratahs.

" Moving to France, he's found out who he is a little bit more and he's come back and he's really connected with the group here and found that bit of mojo that he likes to thrive on," Kiss said.

With English-based Tom Hooper yet to return to the side, Tupou is the only overseas-based Wallaby currently in the Test rotation.

The coach has remained in touch with Racing 92's staff to ensure they have his services for the two-Test tour of Argentina that begins later this month and hopefully beyond.

" All good, as I believe, at this stage.

" I'll be talking to the coach and the team manager of Racing, this week, again, to make sure they understand how we're looking after Nella and making sure we're doing the right thing with him and working him hard.

" So they can trust the process as well. But, yeah, he'll be with us."

Jones joked post-game that Tupou played as if there was a pizza on offer for every try and reckoned he would even deliver one to the change-rooms himself.

" No pizza, I'll have to hit him up about that one," Tupou grinned.

" I've got a lot of love and respect for Eddie, actually. Nothing against that, he loves me, I know that."

Tupou said he wanted to "take it to the next level" after finding his feet in France.

And he said Kiss's tweaks were helping him get there.

" To get the ball in my hands as a forward, less running without the ball, more running with it," Tupou said.

" We're still working on it, but it's good to see forwards scoring tries."
